speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: DISTINGUISHED VISITOR-MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS OF BELGIUM
speechtext:
I have I am sure your permission to note the presence in our galleries of a most distinguished visitor, the minister of foreign affairs of Belgium, Mr. Paul Henri Spaak.
(Translation):
We extend to him the most cordial welcome and wish him a pleasant stay in this country.
(Text):
I need not relate the prodigious career of Mr. Spaak. It is already recorded in history. Suffice it for me to say that we welcome him not only as the outstanding representative of a friendly country but also as one of the greatest diplomats and statesmen of our time. Besides expressing our admiration for his many successful achievements, we pay him a special tribute for his untiring efforts and constant devotion to the cause of world peace.
In asking Mr. Spaak to accept our best wishes we want to assure him of the affection and friendship of the parliament of Canada and of the Canadian people towards his own country and towards the parliament and people of Belgium.
(Translation):
Mr. Spaak, our best wishes and most heartfelt prayers attend you.

subtopic: ARROW LAKES-STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ARROW LAKES-STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
On Tuesday of this week, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) asked me the following question:
In view of assurances given by the minister of lands, forests and mines of British Columbia that an agreement exists between the Bonneville power authority and the Kaiser corporation for the production of power in connection with the proposed Kaiser dam on the Arrow lakes, and in view of the reported statement in Washington by government officials that no agreement exists, is the minister able to give the house any information that will clarify the situation?
I said on Tuesday, sir, that I would try to secure definite information. This morning I received from our embassy in Washington a telegram dated yesterday which reads as follows:
This morning we called on Mr. Morgan D. Dubrow, manager of the Washington office of the Bonneville power authority, to see what information we could obtain at first hand about the relationship between the Kaiser aluminum company and the Bonneville power authority in connection with Kaiser's proposal to build a storage dam on the Arrow lakes.
Mr. Dubrow told us that the Bonneville power authority have signed no contract with the Kaiser aluminum company on their Arrow lakes proposal. He said that the question of a contract had been raised casually by one of Kaiser's executives a few months ago. Later the Kaiser company had made a more definite approach to the Bonneville power authority, saying that it looked as though they would be able to proceed with the construction of a storage dam on the Arrow lakes, and proposing that it might be possible to work out a contract with Bonneville for the generation and distribution of power. They proposed that the contract should provide that, of the additional power which could be generated as a result of storing water in the Arrow lakes, 20 per cent be earmarked for British Columbia and 40 per cent for the Kaiser company. The remaining 40 per cent would go to the Bonneville power authority as payment by Kaiser for the use of the authority's generating facilities. Bonneville power authority's reply was that they would have to think over this proposal before a definite answer could be given. Subsequently a committee made up of representatives from the army corps of engineers, the bureau of reclamation, the federal power commission and the Bonneville power authority was set up in the Pacific northwest for the purpose of reviewing the Kaiser proposal and its implications and reporting on its feasibility.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Last Tuesday, February 22, the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard) asked me the following question:
I should like to ask the Secretary of State when officials of the printing bureau were instructed to send out circular communications and questionnaires to members of parliament in the French language only?
My answer to the question is this. No instructions were given by the queen's printer that circular communications and questionnaires should be sent to members of parliament in the French language only. The hon. member for Wentworth was referring to a circular in the French language concerning the Canada Gazette, part II, a copy of which he was good enough to send to me. Under the authority of an order in council all members of parliament are entitled to receive, free of charge, the Revised Statutes of Canada and the Canada Gazette, part II, in the language they prefer, or in both the English and French editions, as desired and if requested in writing. The name of the hon. member for Wentworth appears on the English list as a member of parliament, and it also appears on the French list because he requested in writing, on November 30, 1953, copies in both languages. The records of the queen's printer indicate that the hon. member for Wentworth

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 3, respecting the construction, operation and maintenance of international river improvements, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Shaw.

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, General McNaughton, the distinguished chairman of the international joint commission, has opposed the Castlegar dam, otherwise called the Kaiser dam, proposed to be built by the Kaiser aluminum company of the United States at Castlegar narrows

at the outlet of the Arrow lakes enlargement of the Columbia river in southeastern B.C. at a point some 20 to 25 miles north of the United States border. It is proposed that this would be built at a cost of from $25 to $30 million. Behind this dam is to be stored 3 million acre feet of Columbia river waters, to be allowed to run down the Columbia in periods of low water and to regulate the flow of the river to enable generating plants downstream in the United States to produce more power. This would be impossible for them without such regulated flow. The Kaiser company have agreed to return to British Columbia 20 per cent of the power made possible by this storage.
Why is General McNaughton anxious about the Castlegar dam? Why does he fear that the project will mean to Canada a loss of her rights in the Columbia river for future generations? This is the great question the house must be able to answer before it can vote intelligently on Bill No. 3 now before us for second reading.
Liberal, Conservative and C.C.F. speakers have held that the house should give the bill second reading and then send it to the committee on external affairs to learn the answer to this question. Social Credit speakers have maintained that the house ought to send the subject matter of the bill to the committee to find the answer before giving the bill second reading and thereby endorsing its principle. The house is now debating an amendment to the motion for second reading moved by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) and seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston). The amendment reads as follows:
That Bill No. 3 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on external affairs.
I support the amendment, Mr. Speaker.
I spoke first on Bill No. 3 on February 10, as reported at pages 1029 to 1036 of Hansard. I spoke again on February 11, as reported at pages 1096 to 1102 of Hansard. This is my third speech on the bill. Consequently I am "filibustering", according to the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
In each of my two former speeches I endeavoured to give a clear picture of the situation pertaining to the Castlegar dam. In this talk I propose to go yet further in shedding light, not heat, on the situation.
The questions we need to ask ourselves are, first, what causes General McNaughton's anxiety concerning the Castlegar dam project? The answer to this question appears to be that the general believes the Castlegar dam project will result in the acquisition by the United States of a greater claim on and

control of Columbia's water than the United States could otherwise establish. If that be the case and there is no way of avoiding it, the matter is quite serious.
The second question is, granted that there might be found to be some urgency relative to the building of Castlegar dam, is there any way whereby British Columbia might neutralize the danger and yet build the dam? If there is not, that is an important matter to be known, too. I think the answer to this second question is yes. I see no convincing reason, nor have I heard any, why the United States, in order to obtain the benefits which would accrue to her through the dam, would not be willing and eager to waive all claims to additional appropriations which might otherwise be hers through the Castlegar dam project.
If that should be found to be true it would pretty well blow the balloon of opposition to smithereens, would it not? I do not see any reason why the United States would not be willing to waive such claims to possible appropriations on the river. Surely in times like these, and in a period when men have attained some degree of intelligence in international relations, especially Canada and the United States, we ought to be able to expect as much as that from the great United States.
The third question is, is there a measure of fundamental urgency relative to the building of the Castlegar dam? I believe the answer to that question must be yes.
Tjie fourth question is, do circumstances at present compelling the British Columbia government render it in high degree necessary for her to have United States private enterprise construct the Castlegar dam? To me it appears that the answer to question No. 4 is yes.
Question No. 5: If so, what could and should be done by the dominion government in connection with this matter? In my opinion the answer to question No. 5 is that the dominion government ought to advance British Columbia necessary financial aid to enable the province to discharge its responsibilities in relation to the construction of the dam and other means of conserving the resources of the Columbia river. I think it would be difficult to show that such is not the case.
Question No. 6: Does the present British Columbia government give evidence of adequate understanding of and alertness to the risks and all other matters involved in the Castlegar dam project, and does that government appear appropriately diligent in its efforts to have the whole situation well in 50433-931
International Rivers
hand, having regard to every aspect of plans and procedures, present and future? Considering the study I have been able to give to the matter I think one can only answer yes. The British Columbia government, as far as I have been able to find out-and I have probed into this matter with some care-give evidence to me of the most thorough preparation and understanding of the whole situation, and are not asleep at the switch in any respect whatsoever.
In my remarks today it will be my aim to present-

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
I said what I thought. If hon. members laugh at it probably some of them do not know enough.
In my remarks today it will be my aim to present to the house and to the country some of my reasons for the answers I have given to these six questions.
May I begin by asking this question. Is Premier Bennett within his rights and his responsibilities when his government proposes and negotiates the Castlegar dam agreement? Hear what General McNaughton said on May 12, 1954, in the external affairs committee when speaking on the Mica creek dam, as recorded at page 174 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of that committee. I read:
The people to build it-
I hat is the Mica dam, in this case. The general continues:
-the responsibility of building that dam, lies with the provincial government. They must say whether ^re going to build it themselves through the British Columbia power commission or whether they are going to bring in a group of private interests to build it. All these things are very definite possibilities, but the decision will lie with the provincial government.
That is point No. 1 that a good many of our over-eager ministers appear to have overlooked.
The next question we need to ask is this. Is Premier Bennett exercising evident circumspection in his handling of the Castlegar project? Is he keeping the situation fluid so the details of the project may be modified? To show that modifications are actually now being contemplated let me quote from the throne debate speech of Mr. Sommers in January, 1955, as follows:
Let me now turn to another facet of this question and that is the consideration being given as to whether the Kaiser company should build a dam or whether the British Columbia government should undertake this phase of the operation. If your government carries through with the building it is expected that extra revenue to the government, in addition to the 60,000 horsepower being developed free for British Columbia, and in addition to tax revenues, will amount to a possible

International Rivers
$600,000 per year income because of provincial financing of the dam. Based on an estimated cost of $30 million, the $600,000 will represent 2 per cent per annum of the investment.
I would like to emphasize that this alternative, in which the province would construct the dam, has been thoroughly reviewed and is disclosed to be a profitable operation. In essence the project could be stated as follows:
1.	The province would charge 6*275 per cent of the cost of the dam as represented by the net proceeds of the sum of money borrowed for this purpose, plus the cost of operation and maintenance (presently estimated at $200,000), and $275,000 in lieu of taxes, plus 60,000 horsepower delivered free to British Columbia.
2.	The Kaiser aluminum company would post an acceptable performance bond to guarantee these payments for 50 years and give adequate assurance of the capability of the Bonneville power administration to deliver its quota of free power to British Columbia over the 50-year period.
3.	The Kaiser aluminum company is required to advise the government of the province if they wish to enter into a new contract on these bases with the province building the dam.
Notice the word "required" there, not "asked", which indicates that the province is completely in control of the situation, notwithstanding some of the extravagant remarks we have heard men make. In this passage we see that a means of construction by the provincial government is being contemplated, having Mr. Kaiser pay for the stored water.
It will be argued that even if British Columbia herself builds the Castlegar dam through the British Columbia power commission and permits	3	million	acre	feet	ofwater to go down the Columbia and be used by United States concerns for the generation of power; that even if the province rather than the Kaiser company does that, the Castlegar dam project will be dangerous to Canada's best interests in the Columbia because primarily	3	million	acre	feet	of
water employed as a means of regulating the flow of the Columbia will result in the construction of greatly increased facilities in the United States and in consequent industrial expansion and greater and greater United States dependence upon Canada's Columbia waters, thereby establishing in the United States a vested right which in effect would give the United States a so-called appropriation on the Columbia in Canada, dangerously increasing their claim beyond that which now, under conditions of high and low water obtaining in the Columbia, they could possibly have.
This appropriation aspect of the whole Castlegar question is well developed in Mr. Barkway's Financial Post article "Water over the Boundary" from which I quoted in my remarks on February 22. I freely grant the probable validity of Mr. Barkway's contention concerning the dangers from United States appropriation on the Columbia as regards
[Mr. Blackmore.l
the Castlegar dam or even the Mica dam, unless appropriate steps are taken by Mr. Sommers and Premier Bennett to safeguard British Columbia and Canada against those dangers.
I feel confident, however, that the British Columbia government has given most careful consideration to every aspect of such dangers of appropriation by the United States, and that the British Columbia government has from United States agencies the most positive assurance-I am not stating that they have, I am simply confident it is so from what I have read-to be followed in due course by adequately binding commitments, obligating the United States as a nation, the individual states affected and all companies and individuals concerned to waive any claim to any appropriation on the Columbia, having regard to the boundary waters treaty of 1909, which might appear to accrue to the United States or any state or states or company or companies or individual by reason of the increased flow of the Columbia resulting from waters stored through the Castlegar dam and in good, neighbourly co-operation permitted to flow into the United States. It would be an astonishing thing if they would not give us a waiver in return for that kind of neighbourliness. I believe they would.
Would the United States be willing to make such binding commitments? It is only simple logic to assume that she would gladly do so rather than deprive herself of the full advantages which, through making such binding commitments, she might enjoy by reason of such full development of the potentialities of the Columbia as could be made possible through the most sincere and unselfish co-operation between the United States and Canada.
The Columbia river is a magnificent asset, extremely valuable to either Canada or the United States working separately, and much more valuable to the two nations working together. The peculiar characteristics of the Columbia river, both in the United States and in Canada, taken together with the special circumstances that surround and have hitherto surrounded British Columbia governments past and present in their efforts to develop the power and water potential of the Columbia river, render it almost if not completely impossible to develop the Columbia adequately except in appropriate co-operation with the United States. British Columbia has understood that; British Columbia now understands that.
The United States urgently requires water in the Columbia with which to generate power. The United States cannot possibly

obtain such water and power except by appropriate co-operation with British Columbia, in the course of which co-operation British Columbia will construct or cause to be constructed in British Columbia dams for storing Columbia river high water to be employed in controlling and regulating the flow of the Columbia downstream. By means of such regulation of flow it is estimated that one-fifth of the total power potential of the Columbia system, estimated at 34 million kilowatts, will be rendered possible, such one-fifth thereby being made available for equitable division between the United States and Canada as upstream and downstream benefits.
One-fifth of 34 million kilowatts is not a matter to be treated lightly on either side of the line, and is not a matter for hectic and exciting remarks. The successful defence of North America could easily depend upon the early adequate development of the full Columbia potential. The United States is aware of that. Our politicians in Canada should become aware of it. Having all these considerations in mind the United States would certainly be cogently motivated to agree to waive all additional appropriation possibilities in order to gain access to Columbia water stored in British Columbia.
What are the peculiar characteristics of the Columbia which render its full development so difficult for British Columbia? Here are the general facts about the Columbia river. The Columbia river rises in British Columbia, traverses parts of British Columbia, Washington, Idaho, Montana and Oregon. Considering the head and flow, the Columbia in terms of hydro power ranks with the largest rivers in the world. Its average annual discharge is about 180 million acre feet. Its drop from the source in British Columbia to the mouth on the Pacific ocean in the United States is 2,652 feet. Of its total flow approximately 44 per cent originates in British Columbia. Of its drop in elevation, approximately 50 per cent occurs in each of Canada and the United States.
The Columbia is primarily a snow-melt stream. Thus the river fluctuates greatly with high flows during spring and summer and low flows during winter. Hence considerable storage of high-flow water is necessary if maximum benefits are to be derived from the Columbia by either Canada or the United States, or both, and there should be storage and maintenance of as nearly as possible a balanced continuous flow.
Recognizing and appreciating the facts of the situation in respect to the Columbia, the Hon. R. E. Sommers, British Columbia minister of lands, forests and mines, in the debate
International Rivers
on the throne speech in the British Columbia legislature on January 19, 1955, said:
Consequently it is apparent that for maximum hydro power production from the stream it is necessary that some portion of the high flows be stored for release during the low flow periods to provide as nearly as possible a balanced, continuous flow through the power-generating installations.
Keeping this in mind, and remembering that Canadian projects will be upstream from an eventual developed head of possibly 1,000 feet in the United States it is easily recognized that any storage development in British Columbia, where we have a similar low flow period to that in the United States, will automatically benefit all installations on the mainstem Columbia below the border. Therefore, it seems essential that full co-operation on an international basis should be sought, such that we operate our installations in conjunction with theirs, to produce maximum power from the resulting system, with agreements for the sharing of the benefits that accrue.
I ask all hon. members and all people across the country who read this, do those words indicate that man lacks in statesmanship? Do they indicate a lack of vision and understanding? Do they indicate any lack of interest or all-round responsibility? Do they indicate irresponsibility? I think only Liberal or C.C.F. politicians will answer in the affirmative.

speechtext: You will see.

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
I know we shall see, and we will not have long to wait. My hon. friends should be trying to understand these things instead of talking nonsense, as are a great many people in the Liberal and Conservative ranks.
The Social Credit government, through the water rights branch of the British Columbia lands service, are participating actively in all phases of planning and development of the Columbia basin. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) gave as the reason for introducing this bill the attainment of orderly development. May I say that they do not need him interfering in their affairs out in British Columbia in order to obtain orderly development. They have been working on that matter for many years already, and they are working on it now. All that is needed is just financial help and a little bit of good sound common sense on the part of the minister in dealing with this matter, and all will be well without this bill.
I read another excerpt from Mr. Sommers' speech:
As investigations and collection of basic data nears completion, certain potential developments become recognized as key sites in the over-all plan. However, the details involved in some of the phases of the planning present many problems and variations, such that several alternative schemes must be studied to determine the most advantageous development.
The map before you-

International Rivers
He had before him an extensive map which I believe I have seen.
-shows the location of known major potential power sites and developments in the Columbia basin in British Columbia as well as the hydropower installations which have been constructed. The at-site power development should be in an orderly sequence following creation of the necessary storage and regulated flow.
The minister was not the first to talk about orderly development. I continue:
Such storage can be adequately provided in the Arrow lakes and behind the proposed Mica dam. The orderly sequences of at-site power development may then be undertaken in the following order, and in point of fact, in some instances could be developed concurrently:
1.	Bring Waneta No. 1 up to its full capacity of
500.000	h.p. by the installation of two additional generators.
2.	Waneta No. 2 to be developed giving an additional 500,000 h.p.
3.	Mica at-site power 800,000 h.p.
4.	Downie creek at-site power 500,000 h.p.
5.	Little Dalles at-site power 300,000 h.p.
6.	Murphy creek, valueless without the Mica and Arrow lakes storage, however with this storage it will give at-site power of 130,000 h.p. without any loss of head at Brilliant.
Although Surprise rapids and Donald canyon sites are marked on the map, they do not appear to be very practical at this time due to the dislocation of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the fact that there is every indication that the Mica dam should be a high-head installation.
All the suggested installed capacities mentioned above would be subject to increase provided Canadian and American power systems were interconnected and the over-all generation made to the best advantage of the large grid.
Once more I ask this question. Does that sound like the words of an irresponsible person?
In this quotation we learn that at present under active consideration in the Columbia river Canadian section there are six major power sites awaiting development. To restate them, we have Waneta No. 1 with
500.000	h.p.; Waneta No. 2 with 500,000 h.p.; Mica with 800,000 h.p.; Downie creek with
500.000	h.p.; Little Dalles with 300,000 h.p. and Murphy creek with 130,000 h.p., a total of 2,730,000 h.p.
Mr. Sommers states that storage necessary to supply all these projects can be provided by two dams, at Mica creek and Arrow lakes.
How can the province of British Columbia manage to bring about the construction of the dams required to provide storage for these two projects first, as a provincial project; second, through private enterprise? The study of this particular question has a great bearing upon the attitude we shall adopt towards the Castlegar dam.
From the quotation from General McNaugh-ton which I read earlier in my present remarks it is recognized as being the duty of British Columbia to construct necessary dams on the Columbia river, or to manage to have them constructed.
By what means can British Columbia accomplish this task? Could she do so by public ownership, by doing the job directly herself? What the minister said in that one quotation I read indicated that he might be considering doing that, but under ordinary circumstances the danger to the British Columbia debt situation would be great.
Let us consider the Mica dam. Its cost is estimated at $425 million. There is some discrepancy, but this is the figure I have had given me. The total revenue of British Columbia for the year ended March 31, 1954 was $169,033,874. Expenditures were $165,624,160. The total estimated revenue for the year ending March 31, 1956, is $194,522,469; estimated expenditures are $211,814,341. The net public debt as of December 31, 1954, was $139,370,142.24. Will any member of this house argue that British Columbia could safely commit herself to the staggering additional debt of $425 million?
I shall be reminded that the Mica dam when completed will be capable of supporting installations able to generate an estimated 800,000 horsepower and so will be self-liquidating. I point out that in the area contiguous to the Mica dam in British Columbia there is already a surplus of 75,000 kilowatts for sale, and the potential of an additional 250,000 horsepower easily and readily made available at Waneta No. 1 plant, and another easily and readily made available 500,000 horsepower at Waneta No. 2 site.
When I then ask my friend where and to whom the 800,000 horsepower coming from Mica dam would be sold, I shall probably be told that United States companies-perhaps the Kaiser Aluminum and Chemical Corporation-will come into that area of British Columbia and establish industries, once being assured of adequate supplies of cheap power. Perhaps, but by no means certainly. Or I shall be told that since power can now be transmitted as far as 600 miles it might be feasible to sell this power from Mica to Calgary or to Vancouver or to some other place. Again perhaps. But would anyone in this house, if he were premier of British Columbia, commit that province to an obligation of $425 million which could so easily result in utter financial disaster, merely to discharge a responsibility to build Columbia water storage? No, he would not! I do not care whether he is the youngest man or the oldest man in the house.
Obviously if British Columbia as a province is to develop the Columbia river as to power and as to water, then British Columbia will have to be afforded financial help by the dominion government, and that

in extremely generous measure. She does not need acts like this one at present before us.
Why should not British Columbia receive ample help in protecting Canadian rights on the Columbia? Alberta, after far too much delay on Ottawa's part, finally was given financial help in saving for future Canadians what was left of Canada's rich heritage in the St. Mary river, and now the Belly and Waterton rivers, precious international streams in southern Alberta, as well as other rivers in Alberta. Saskatchewan has asked, and in due time will receive, liberal dominion help in preserving her Saskatchewan river. That is quite as it ought to be. Let British Columbia be granted without any further hesitation all the financial help she needs to save for Canada the priceless treasures of the Columbia. Let her be granted all the money she needs for this task, I say, without any strings attached in any way, shape or form.
Let us bear in mind how that noble sovereign sister province, in the propitious year of 1871, gave herself to our union, making this nation possible with the help of divine Providence. Shame on all unworthy Canadians who are this day conspiring to rob her of her freedoms in return for a niggardly bit of help in connection with the Columbia river. Because of this federal government's neglect she has had to turn to foreign private interests for aid in protecting the Columbia. That explains the present Castlegar dam proposal. I wonder how the shoe feels to be put on the right foot?
Second, can British Columbia successfully develop these power and water resources through private ownership, as she is attempting to do in the case of Castlegar? Does the minister know of any Canadian or British financial company that would be likely to build Mica dam and the generating plant required? We will certainly welcome an answer in the affirmative. What offers of American help have been received by British Columbia? It may be that several offers have been made. I have not as yet had time to investigate thoroughly enough to be able to say.
Here, however, is one. According to a Seattle Canadian Press dispatch appearing in the Nelson Daily News of December 8, 1954, the Puget Sound utilities council offered to build Mica creek dam, spending $250 million upon it, storing an estimated
10,500,000	acre feet of water, about twice that of Grand Coulee dam, in return for the additional electricity that could be generated
International Rivers
in United States plants with the water conserved behind the dam and sent down the river through regulated flow.
An official of that council had said that the council's proposal to construct the Mica dam would give British Columbia the "cheapest power in the United States or Canada."

It would then come back to the house and hon. members would then be able to face a vote on second reading and assert conscientiously that they were fully conscious of the implications involved. That is the position we find it necessary to take at this time.
The hon. member is quite incorrect in suggesting that the bill would come back to the house. In this connection I must remind the house that in the session of 1944 Bill No. 109, an act to incorporate the Alberta provincial bank, was introduced by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), and after he had moved second reading an amendment was then moved by a former minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, in the following terms:
That this bill be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the select standing committee on banking and commerce for consideration and report.
The amendment was accepted, yeas 93, nays 20. At that time the nays were of course the members of the Social Credit group. What was the result of that amendment? There was no consideration of the principle of the bill. Nobody ever heard any more about the bill in the house after that.
I suggest that if the present amendment were accepted it would have the same effect on the bill now under discussion. It would mean that the bill would be killed. We in this group are not in favour of killing the bill.

International Rivers
The whole attitude again indicates that the government of the United States recognized the fact that in dealing with this problem they have to deal with the government of Canada in the first instance. When we are dealing with problems of this nature they have to be dealt with on a national level because they involve matters concerning external affairs. This principle has been accepted in Canada up to the present time.
On the basis of that understanding this government has spent something in the neigh-Dourhood of $3 million on investigations of the Columbia river basin. This government's engineers and the engineers of the federal authorities in the United States have been co-operating for the past 10 years, working toward the development of a plan that would be mutually advantageous to both countries, and advantageous to British Columbia. This procedure, this practice and this expenditure, in my opinion, have been entirely overlooked by this piecemeal approach to the development of the river proposed by British Columbia.
It seems to me it must be obvious to anyone that when the government of the United States wishes to give effect to programs related to international rivers, it must deal with the government of Canada. Therefore, in our opinion, this legislation is certainly necessary to protect the national interest and permit the federal government to exercise its responsibility without question.
I want to deal with one other matter before concluding. I am not speaking at length this afternoon. During this debate it has been stated repeatedly that this bill is an invasion of provincial rights. I am quite sure the hon. gentlemen to my left are quite sincere in that criticism. I believe that is their major argument, that this proposal is an invasion of provincial rights. We cannot agree with them. I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that in addition to provincial rights there are such things as regional, local and individual rights. The agreement between the government of British Columbia and the Kaiser corporation was signed without any consultation or interchange of views with the appropriate representatives of local governments or individuals concerned in my area. They were simply told of this development being proposed after the agreement was signed.
I want to bring to the attention of the house, Mr. Speaker, the fact that in the development of the Columbia in the United States an entirely different, and in my opinion more democratic, practice prevails. Every consideration has been given to the rights and the views of the people directly concerned.
[Mr. Herridge.l
Naturally in my district there are a lot of people who are directly concerned with this development because of its effect on their property, their rights and their interests. There are a lot of people who are opposed to the proposed Kaiser dam because it would mean appropriation by a private company of Canadian waters.
I might explain that when I spoke last I mentioned that to my knowledge there was not a single organization in my riding that was in favour of this proposal. I must say, to be quite fair, that since I last spoke the Castlegar board of trade has endorsed this proposal. That is quite understandable. This municipality is below the dam, so that is quite natural. It is possible if the dam is built there will be $25 or $30 million expended near that community. That may have some effect on opinions concerning the matter. I can say this, that from the point where the dam is to be built north to Revelstoke there is strong opposition.
In support of my statement that the practice in the United States in my opinion is somewhat more democratic, I want to quote from Bill H. R. 4286, the Columbia valley administration act, which was introduced in 1949 by Mr. Mitchell. I do this to indicate that there are such things as regional, local and individual rights, as well as provincial rights. At page 6 of the bill we find this:
State and Local Participation
Section 5. The administration-
This means, of course, the federal administration in the United States.
-shall seek the advice, assistance, and participation of the people of the region and their state and local governments and organizations, public and private, to the fullest practicable extent, in the formulation and execution of programs designed to carry out the purposes of this act. To this end, the administration shall make arrangements for consultation and interchange of views with appropriate representatives of state and local governments, of the agricultural (including reclamation and irrigation), labor and business interests and of the general public of the region. The administration shall make arrangements for such consultation and interchange of views with respect to all phases of its activities and at all appropriate places throughout the region, and shall establish such advisory boards and councils (including at least boards or councils concerned with irrigation and reclamation, power, fishery resources, and navigation) as may be necessary or appropriate to achieve the objectives of this section. Any advisory board or council may submit for inclusion in the annual report of the board its comments in summary form on those policies of the administration with which it is concerned, and such comments shall be included in the annual report. For the periods during which they consult with the administration away from their regular places of work, such representatives and members of such boards and councils may receive their actual travelling expenses and a per diem allowance not to exceed $10 in lieu of subsistence.

I suggest that Bill No. 3 makes it possible to give effect to similar procedure in Canada. This bill offers an opportunity for co-operation between federal and provincial governments, and the full consideration of regional, local and individual rights and interests. I think it is only fair to say that, as I heard them, the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated clearly that he is approaching the problem in that spirit.
Wherever the natural level of any river or lake was to be changed by any works on that river or lake, in Canada or in the United States, it has been the practice for the international joint commission to hold meetings in the area concerned, and to listen to the representations made by local organizations or individuals. I want to illustrate just how democratically the international joint commission has operated. They have not allowed anyone to erect a dam or to flood any property without holding a meeting in the area concerned and listening to the representations of farmers, labour organizations and individuals.
I shall illustrate that in two ways. Some years ago an application was made to raise the level of Kootenay lake. The hearing was held at Creston. In fact two meetings were held, one at Creston and one at Nelson. Farmer representatives made representations; labour representatives made representations; and individuals living along the lake who thought their foreshore rights would be affected were there. I attend most of the meetings in my area, and I know that in particular I attended this one. I was very much impressed by the fact that the chairman of the Canadian section of the international joint commission very patiently listened to what was said, and particularly to one old gentleman who could not express himself 50433-944
International Rivers
very loudly but was very much concerned that his foreshore might be flooded unnecessarily.
The commission listened carefully to the representations of Creston farmers concerning the raising of the lake level and the water table under their fields. Before any order was granted by the international joint commission for the raising of the water level the people in the area were satisfied that the farmers in the Creston district were to be properly compensated, and the complaints of persons around the lake who thought they might be affected in the foreshore area of their property were properly looked into. The commission has been most careful to consider the interests of local organizations and individuals. I give that as an illustration of the work of a commission operating under the sponsorship of the federal government, a commission taking great care to protect the rights of the local people.
In addition I want to draw the attention of the house to the attitude of another federal department when doing anything that affects the rights or interests of organizations or individuals. I have found during a period of nearly 50 years that the federal Department of Public Works is most considerate in that respect. If the federal department is going to erect a structure which will change the flow of a stream or divert the flow of water so that land will be eroded, docks affected, private wharfage affected or booming grounds affected, the federal Department of Public Works to my personal knowledge over a period of 50 years has always made certain that local representations have been heard and local interests were protected. And if this work had to be undertaken, then the necessary crib work and mattresses were put in to protect the property line from erosion, and to protect the interests of everyone concerned.
I mention these facts to bring out the point that in addition to provincial rights there are regional, local and individual rights. My argument is that in my personal experience over the past 50 years it has been clearly indicated to me that wherever any department or agency of the federal government had to deal with problems which might affect regional, local or individual interests, they have been most careful to see that those interests have been protected.
When this bill is passed, surely we can expect this same protection and the same consideration of regional, local and individual interests. Sir, we in this group are particularly opposed to the appropriation of Canadian waters in international rivers by United States private interests. Once again I repeat.

International Rivers
we hope that the early development of the Columbia river power and storage potential at Mica creek will result from co-operation between the federal and provincial governments and the government of the United States.
I trust this measure will soon receive second reading, and that members of the external affairs committee will soon have an opportunity to commence the hearing of witnesses, the taking of evidence and the study and investigation of many problems of constitutional-in some people's minds-engineering, financial, regional, local and individual matters, so that when this bill finally becomes law we will have laid the foundation for satisfactory and permanent co-operation between federal and provincial governments for the development of the potential of the Columbia river to the mutual advantage of all concerned both in Canada and the United States.

Mr. Speaker, it seems my lot in this debate to have the privilege of following the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). This afternoon I have a confession to make. Apparently he and I are ex-Liberals. The only difference between us is that quite often he forgets the party to which he owes allegiance at the present time, whereas there is no doubt whatever in my mind.
However, I am also pleased to note that there is a certain softening in his speech this afternoon in comparison with what was given to the house a few nights ago. There is a stronger plea for co-operation with the provincial government. I spoke on this subject on a previous occasion, Mr. Speaker. I believe that my speech was based entirely on a plea for a provincial and federal conference to settle this dispute. I have no apology for anything I said at that time, and I have learned nothing since to make me sorry that I took the stand I did.
At the present time we are speaking to an amendment. That amendment is to the effect that we delay second reading of the bill at this time and that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on external affairs. I am not an old timer in this house, but in the short time I have been here I have become convinced that once the principle of a bill is approved by this house, any amendments made in committee or elsewhere are of minor importance. We believe, Mr. Speaker, that this bill is too vital and too important to go before a committee at this time, where we can expect very few, or at the most, minor, changes.

I have been reading a good deal about this whole subject in the last few days. I read an article by Mr. Minifie; I read an article by Bruce Hutchison; I read an article by Senator Reid, and I noticed a big heading as follows:	"Kaiser bill one of the biggest
steals". We read both sides of the question, Mr. Speaker, and by so doing we hope to arrive at a conclusion which to our minds is just and fair. We have heard and we have learned quite a lot about the general and popular feeling in the minds of the people of British Columbia and of Canada since this bill came into the spotlight.
Before going on to some of these things I am going to refer to the answer which was given today by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) to the hon. member for Kootenay West. The answer and the text of that telegram imprinted upon my mind more fully than ever the fact that this matter is in such a stage of negotiation and is so vitally important to the United States, Canada and the province of British Columbia that no step should be taken at this -time that is going to endanger the results we hope to get by such negotiation.
In connection with the article, I might say that I came to the catty-should I use that WOrd-conclusion that the United States government, in putting forth a plea for negotiation with the federal government over the Columbia development, thought possibly they could drive a better bargain with the federal government than with the government of British Columbia. I cite the St. Lawrence seaway proposition as a case in point.
I have some other articles here that confirm our stand that there is too much indecision in this matter before it can be brought to a speedy end. The hon. member who preceded me referred to the decision of the Castlegar board of trade. Unfortunately he does not consider their opinion of too much importance, and he passed it off by saying, "Well, they are below the dam and it would affect them in no great way." I believe that boards of trade throughout Canada, not only at Castlegar, give pretty fair consideration to problems that are placed before them for attention.
Right here I should like to put on record the fact that a board of trade in my own riding-and I am referring to the city of Vernon board of trade-held a meeting in November which I attended. The question of the Castlegar dam was brought up. There is a division of opinion, and we are not denying that fact; but at this board of trade meeting they decided to set up a committee to

get the facts and the data on this project before they would pass an opinion on it. They have not yet arrived at a conclusion, because as soon as they had reached a decision I was to be advised.
I should like you to know, Mr. Speaker, that the decision at which the Castlegar board of trade arrived was the result of the deliberations of the committee which was set up some months ago. It is a serious question that requires a lot of study. Apparently, the people of British Columbia are giving it that study. Therefore, we are asking that action be delayed with respect to endorsing the principle of this bill until all the facts are before us.
I hold in my hand an editorial which appeared in the Times of February 11, as follows:
Last night in Rossland a spokesman for the Kaiser aluminum company gave the first public defence of that company's actions in the Arrow lakes power deal with the provincial government. Robert A. Sandberg, who is a public relations expert for the company, gave the Rossland chamber of commerce a reasoned and intelligent summary of Kaiser's part in the negotiations.

We suggest that many other groups in the district would profit from hearing the Kaiser case.
I quote this, Mr. Speaker, just to bring to the attention of this house the fact that the people of British Columbia are alive to the serious problem with which they are faced, and are giving it their very best attention.

As was mentioned in the house the other night, in the southern part of my riding there are many problems connected with irrigation. Just stop and think what this legislation will mean. Any person who wanted to establish a little dam to irrigate his land would have to find out where that water eventually found its way, whether it went into the United States or through Canada into the Pacific or even into the Arctic. It would affect irrigation projects, domestic water supply, domestic power supply; all those things which are of such vital importance in the southern and western parts of my riding.
My opposition to this bill is based more and more on the belief that the centralization of power in Ottawa is a serious thing. I believe in the rights of the provinces, in provincial autonomy. I believe that legislation

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate on second reading of this bill commenced on February 4, I outlined the stand of this party. It may be summed up again to this effect. We believe that this bill should be sent to a committee. As a matter of fact, during the debate on the throne speech, I suggested that that course be followed. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has eventually agreed to that suggestion. As Your Honour knows, he has stated that the bill will go to the standing committee on external affairs.
Our stand was sincerely taken because we believe that this measure is one which is ideal for study by a committee. It is perfectly obvious that, no matter how long debate goes on in this house, we are all talking of things about which we know very little. Perhaps we do that on other occasions as well. However, here is a case where the evidence of experts is needed before any member of this house is qualified to say whether or not the
International Rivers
bill is a good one. When it goes to a committee General McNaughton and officials of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources can be called. If the British Columbia government really wants to have the merits considered, it can send its own experts here to give evidence and can arrange to have the Kaiser people send witnesses as well. No one has suggested that the hearings of the committee will not be practically wide open. The Minister of Trade and Commerce gave that intimation the other night. I have no reason to question the fact that, when the hearings are held, an honest attempt will be made to get the facts. Then it will be possible for members to decide what they think about this bill.
In my earlier speech I pointed out that we did not consider ourselves bound to support the bill throughout, even though it was given second reading. When it has been considered by a committee and has been reported back to the house, we will then take our stand on the merits of the bill after we have had the opportunity to study the merits and the demerits.
But what is the question before the house this afternoon? It is a motion by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), both from the province of Alberta. It is really touching to see the solicitude of Alberta members for our province of British Columbia. Six of them have taken part in this debate and one of them, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), has made three 40-minute speeches, all purporting to protect British Columbia. The unfortunate fact is that many of the Alberta members, I am afraid, are of the opinion that my native province is now a colony of Alberta. That may be one reason why they are rushing in to protect us from all comers. However, this amendment reads as follows:
That Bill No. 3 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on external affairs.
That is the third amendment moved by the Social Credit party. The first amendment was that the principle of the bill be referred to a dominion-provincial conference. That amendment was ruled out of order. Then as an amendment they moved the six-months' hoist. Of course, if passed, it would have killed the bill. From the speeches that have been made in the debate on the present amendment it is quite evident that the real purpose is again to kill the bill.
Under these circumstances we do not propose to support the amendment, for two reasons. In the first place, if the amendment is carried it means delay and more delay. In

International Rivers
the second place, should it be carried the result would be that the actual terms of the bill could not be considered by the external affairs committee. We believe that it is of great importance that they should be dealt with very carefully in that committee.
I emphasize first the objection to delay. Here is a case where a dispute has developed between the two governments. There have been blasts and counter-blasts. There was a blast in the house the other night by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) which in my opinion was unfortunate. This question is not going to be settled by fiery speeches from any part of the house. Sooner or later the two governments must get together if the Columbia river system is to be developed to the maximum extent possible, and, believe me, that is where the real interests of the people of British Columbia lie, in getting the Columbia river system adequately developed.
I do not believe there are many people in British Columbia who are much interested in the fight that is going on between the two governments. They are concerned about the proper type of development being undertaken. That is quite impossible if the dominion government and the government of British Columbia cannot reach agreement. I need only point out what has happened with regard to the development of power on the St. Lawrence river in connection with the seaway scheme. There you have the province of Ontario co-operating with the dominion government. You have a huge scheme going ahead with everybody working together, and the result is going to be that the province of Ontario and the nation as a whole will derive the maximum benefit from this development.
That is what must be done with the Columbia river system. There again is a huge power potential. It will mean as much or more to the people of British Columbia, not only those of the present generation but of future generations, as any development that has ever taken place in the west coast province. Here there is a vast potential project. Everyone who was a member of the external affairs committee last year was impressed by the evidence given by General McNaughton as to the possibilities of the Columbia river. This river constitutes a challenge to both the government of the dominion and the government of the province of British Columbia. I do not believe it is in the best interests of any Canadian that the whole project should be held up by talk in the house or by a failure of the two governments to get together. The longer we delay, the more loose talk there is going to be and the more 
friction will develop between the two governments. There has been far too much already, and I am hoping that the bill can be sent to the committee today and that next week we can start hearing the expert witnesses.
Our other objection is that if this motion carries the terms of the bill cannot be considered in the committee. For example, there is the definition of an international river. The Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources told us that there were some 20 rivers in Canada which would come under the definition of an international river. We must study that definition. Then there is the definition of an international river improvement which is even more important because it is more complicated and more difficult. We must find out what sort of improvements on international rivers are to come under the bill. Then there are the provisions for forfeiture, for the seizing of works and for penalties, all of which require study because they are provisions which might lead to very serious trouble in this country.
Again, there is the application of the bill to works already in existence. There are many works on the Columbia river at the present time, and apparently they will come under the terms of the bill. That question too must be studied by the committee. Then there is the constitutional question, the whole issue of whether the bill is constitutional or whether parts of it are and other parts are not. The external affairs committee can go a long way towards solving that problem by calling the law officers and getting their reasons for drawing the bill in the terms in which it has been presented to the house. We believe that a study of the actual terms of the bill is of the utmost importance, and for that reason too we want to see the bill go to the committee and go there just as quickly as possible.
I repeat the stand of the Progressive Conservative party. It is that we reserve our right to oppose further progress of the bill in the house if we should find, as a result of the hearings in the committee, that the bill is unsound. But for the time being until it has been studied by the committee we believe that the proper course is to have it go to the committee and go there just as quickly as possible.

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am the third of the four speakers who have risen this afternoon on the question now before us to state that it was not my intention to speak twice on the matter. However, because of certain statements, and information which has reached me today, 1 feel it imperative that I again enter this debate, f, sir, am opposed to the amendment now before us.
Although this is only my second session in the House of Commons, I have had 24 sessions' experience in a provincial legislature so I believe I know something about procedure. A motion to refer a bill to a committee leaves the bill within the control of the house. A motion to decline second reading of a bill and refer only the subject matter to a committee is exactly the same as a hoist motion; it is a motion to kill the bill. I do
International Rivers
not support any contention that this bill should be killed. I want to say in all sincerity that if the hon. members who belong to the Social Credit group, who have remarked that they are interested in truth and in facts, were really interested in truth and in facts they would not be moving this amendment. They would not be speaking as they are. They would want to get this motion for second reading through so that the bill could be referred to the external affairs committee, where they would have power to call for persons and papers and get the evidence they say they want.
Now, sir, I sincerely hope this bill will get to the committee just as speedily as possible. I hope that at a very early meeting of the committee, the committee will send out an invitation to the government of British Columbia to come down and give their facts and give their evidence. I would hope also that the committee would send a particular request to the minister of lands and forests of British Columbia to come down and give evidence. I have, sir, a particular reason for hoping that the minister of lands and forests will appear before the external affairs committee when that committee deals with this matter.
On February 10 of this year I spoke on this subject and I had this to say as reported at page 1026 of Hansard, about two-thirds of the way down the first column:
One oi the first questions I asked was the matter raised by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr Byrne) a few moments ago. What is the relationship in this matter with the Bonneville power authority? The minister told me they had seen the agreement signed between the kaiser corporation and the Bonneville power interests. Although there is no mention of that in the contract, such an agreement is in existence.
I said that, Mr. Speaker, and the Hansard report is correct. As I explained when I spoke on February 10, knowing this matter was going to come up in the House of Commons, and being a member representing a constituency in British Columbia, I went to Victoria. I saw the premier, and I saw the minister of lands and forests. I asked for the fullest possible information as to their viewpoint and the facts on this proposal of Kaiser to build a dam in the Columbia river. I said, sir, that in my conversation with the minister only once did he say that something was in confidence. What he told me in confidence I have kept confidential. When I spoke on February 10, I gave a true picture of what the minister told me concerning the background and facts related to the view of the government of British Columbia. Sir, standing here in my place as a member of

International Rivers
the House of Commons I say that the statement which I made on February 10, as covered by the Hansard report, page 1026, is correct.
This morning I received, airmail and special delivery, a letter from the Hon. R. E. Sommers, minister of lands and forests in British Columbia. I want, sir, to place this on the record because somebody is guilty of a terminological inexactitude and it is not I. This, sir, I will file with you. The letter I received reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Winch:
I have been following the debates on Bill No. 3 in the House of Commons very closely.
On page 1026 of Hansard 1 noticed that you quoted me as having informed you that I had seen a signed agreement between the Kaiser corporation and the Bonneville power administration relating to possible water storage in the Arrow lakes. There must be some misunderstanding on this point, as I am sure that what I did tell you. was that I had seen a signed letter from the Bonneville administration stating, that it believed that a satisfactory agreement could be worked out with the Kaiser corporation relative to this matter. I have attached a copy of this letter in order to clarify my verbal statement to you.
I know that with your many years experience as a legislator you would, naturally, realize that British Columbia would not issue a conditional water licence to Kaiser unless British Colvunbia was satisfied that an agreement had been signed between the Bonneville administration and the Kaiser corporation, and no water licence has as yet been issued.
I do hope this will set the record straight and I remain,
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) R. E. Sommers.
I want to reiterate here what I said on February 10. I state right now that I asked the minister of lands and forests if there was any arrangement between the Kaiser corporation and Bonneville on power, because, on the basis of his own statements in the press and by radio, Kaiser would get 40 per cent of the power produced, Bonneville would get 40 per cent and British Columbia 20 per cent. There had to be some understanding, so I am going to state very clearly and concisely the answer I got: "The question you raise, Mr. Winch, was one which we considered, and I told the Kaiser representatives that they had to prove to me that they had an understanding, an agreement with Bonneville, otherwise the deal was off." He said, "Shortly thereafter, in my own office here in Victoria, the Kaiser representatives came back and gave me what to me was conclusive proof that they had an understanding, they had an agreement with the Bonneville power corporation." That, sir, is a fact. Yet this morning, I get this letter. I did not see the letter which I now have on the day that I saw the minister of lands and forests in British Columbia. This morning, he sends me a copy of it.

I want to place this letter on the record, too. The letter is headed, "United States Department of the Interior, Bonneville Power Administration, Portland 8, Oregon: Office of the Administrator, August 26, 1954." It reads:
Mr. Norman L. Krey Manager Northwest Operations Kaiser Aluminum and Chemical Corporation 5C5 Spokane and Eastern building Spokane 1. Washington.
Dear Mr. Krey:
This is to confirm the information previously given to you by me concerning the Bonneville power administration's position with respect to the construction of a dam at Arrow lakes to provide for storage of Columbia river flows. We have been consulting with you in regard to this matter since early this year, ever since you first approached the British Columbia government with respect to the possibility of such construction. We have also had conversations with other interested parties. We have been unwilling to make any commitments with respect to our position concerning an Arrow lakes dam until all of the facts in connection with such construction become available. We are of course anxious to see the Arrow lakes construction proceed and believe that we will be able to work out satisfactory arrangements with you for the allocation of the increased federal prime power if you are successful in your negotiations with the British Columbia government. Our preliminary analysis indicates that there is a possibility of the costs in connection with the storage and in connection with the additional facilities for the generation and transmission of power from this storage being met by the sale of the power at reasonable rates.
We will be interested in hearing more concerning your negotiations with the British Columbia government.
(Sgd.) William A. Pearl, Administrator.
Sir, when I spoke on February 10 I tried to give what I thought was a fair presentation of the position of the British Columbia government. But, sir, as time goes on we learn things. I received this letter this morning from the minister of lands and forests. I presume therefore that it is the latest information dealing with the position of the Bonneville power administration itself. And it means what? It could mean only this, that the government of British Columbia has had no understanding and has no authority whatsoever, and does not know the amount of power it could get back if this dam went through. Because, according to Mr. Pearl, the administrator of this corporation, they have made no commitments. And there has been no decision whatsoever as to what they want for the generation of power.
And yet, sir, if this is the document that Sommers told me about in the middle of December then, on the basis of a document of August 26 in which there is no agreement and nothing definite, only one month later- on September 17-the province of British Columbia signed a contract with the Kaiser people. On what basis could they sign any

contract? On what basis could they sign a contract, when the only company that can generate the power says, on August 26: we have made no commitments?
In view of the fact that I received this letter from Mr. Sommers this morning, and a copy of the letter of August 26 from Mr. Pearl, I have an idea that the political tail of Mr. Sommers is now in the gate, and that vocally he is trying to weasel his way out.
There is only one way in which this can be answered now-there is only one way. And it is not from the floor of the House of Commons. That way is by passing the second reading of this bill so that it may be referred to a committee with power to call for persons and papers. And if my hon. friends on my left are sincere they will ask that this motion be now put in order to get it in front of that committee so that not only they but the government of British Columbia car* come on down here to Ottawa and either put up or shut up.
And, sir, may I conclude with this-and I think I have been pretty fair all along in what I have said-that a committee of the House of Commons not only has power to call for persons and papers but also, I believe, has the right to subpoena. And, sir, if those who say that we are invading provincial rights, and that the government is playing politics, do not voluntarily come down here, then I suggest, sir, that we subpoena them.

I am very pleased that we get support from somewhere in the house, because most certainly we cannot depend upon members from British Columbia to give us any, in the discussion on this bill. Apparently, to begin with, they are biased. Hon. members outside the Social Credit group have taken the view that we are here for

only one purpose, that of setting up a filibuster. An hon. member across the way mentioned only a short time ago that that is so, and I have seen similar references in the newspapers recently.
Mr. Speaker, we, too, want the facts. And because we do not happen to have as many members on the external affairs committee as do the other parties, we shall have only one opportunity to present our case as we see it, and that is from the floor of the House of Commons. Of course that does not apply with the same force to the two individuals from this group who are on the external affairs committee. subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext: Even education.

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
And my good friend from Saskatoon says, "Even education"; and how right he happens to be! I would draw this fact to the government's attention. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) asked the question: Did Mr. Bennett ever ask for the advice of this government? The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) answered the question a bit earlier. If he had only taken the trouble to listen he would have heard that the United States federal authorities sought the advice of the state rather than the federal authority itself trying to discover whether or not it was within their jurisdiction. Up to this time, Mr. Speaker, the province of British Columbia has never been denied the right of development along other rivers or this river in particular. It will be recalled that earlier in this debate we discovered that the Skagit river was one of the first to be developed and there was no interference from the federal or any other authority.
In respect to the obstruction of this particular legislation and the so-called filibuster that we are accused of carrying on, I would say this. There are two or three specific purposes behind our speaking in the debate. The

International Rivers
first one the Minister of Trade and Commerce answered the other evening. We were endeavouring to get an admission from the government that they would give to the province of British Columbia an understanding that this bill, if it does become law, will permit the agreement to be consummated. I am willing to take the minister's words for that. Apparently, there is some doubt in his own mind. There is great doubt in the mind of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), that the deal depends upon its own validity. I am not here to discuss and I have never discussed the validity of any Kaiser proposal, or of the provincial deals with them. Our object is to decide whether responsibility rests with the provincial authority or the federal authority, so that we can go home and say that we have a fair deal, if it is at all possible to get one. There are other purposes behind our bringing up this question at this time. The first question is the constitutionality of the bill and the other is provincial rights, and our responsibility as members of parliament.
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Red Deer has been read several times. I shall read it again:
That Bill No. 3 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on external affairs.
This amendment has served one purpose, if no other, namely, it has established that the government recognizes the possibility that the Kaiser-British Columbia deal is a fair and good one. It has served a worthwhile purpose in so far as the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is concerned.
However, we need to discover the legality of this particular bill and the authority upon which it is based. In that connection, section 92, subsection 10, of the B.N.A. Act deals with certain rights which have been assigned to the provinces and to the federal authorities. Paragraph (a) of subsection 10 reads as follows:
Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province.
These are assigned to the federal authority. One thing that strikes me as being very important is the question of railways. If railways come under the federal authority, are they not of national interest? Why have we not a bill to take over the Pacific Great Eastern Railway? I bring that in to indicate that it is an important factor. We are told from time to time by hon. members of the government that they have that authority vested in them by section 92 of the British Nor :h America Act. Is it not in the national

interest, Mr. Speaker, to conserve the forests and forest products? Would it not be just as simple for this government to say that they were going to take over all the forest industries in Canada? We have forests in every province, and not in just one particular province. Should they not also, in the national interest, take over flooding? In 1943, in my particular part of British Columbia, the lowlands were flooded. The federal authorities came to our assistance. They did not pass legislation saying that all districts that are subject to flooding come under the federal authority. They tried in every way to avoid that. Whenever they get a chance to avoid spending a dollar you may be sure they will do it.
What about the conservation of iron ore in Quebec? That surely would be in the national interest. In 50 years or 100 years from now we may have a terrific industry in iron. Why should that not come under the national authority? I am sure that my friends of the C.C.F. party would say: "Let us nationalize everything". This Social Credit group does not stand for nationalization of anything unless we feel that the national good of the nation as a whole would be helped by carrying on that industry when it becomes necessary. We pass on to private enterprise the carrying on of industry wherever that is possible.
