speechtext:
No. I would suggest that the minister would help the people of British Columbia more if he introduced a bill saying that it is in the interest of the nation to extend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act into my province and particularly into my area.
I contend, sir, as I said earlier, that up to a certain point, when this government finds it in the national interest to make the provinces and the municipal districts pay heavy taxes, they do so; but it is not in the national interest when they have to expend any more money than is absolutely necessary in any one of the provinces to try to help them get along. As 1 say, at that point co-operation seems to end.

I come now to the principal question on this bill. Will any province besides British Columbia be affected? How will it affect the people of Alberta? They have the St. Mary river dam today. Is it going to change Alberta in any respect, or the revenue of Alberta? I say no. In Saskatchewan they have the Souris river and the Frenchman river. Is it going to affect that province? Can we develop power or anything else there? It is not going to affect New Brunswick-no, not those people. It is not going to affect Ontario. It is not going to affect Quebec and Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island or Manitoba. It is going to affect just one province, British Columbia, and it is in the national interest that this national government should take it over; at least that is what we are given to understand.
Where are our champions of free enterprise?

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext: And of freedom?

subtopic: PROVISION REQUIRING LICENCE FROM GOVERNMENT OF CANADA TO CONSTRUCT, OPERATE AND MAINTAIN ANY IMPROVEMENT
speechtext:
The essence of free enterprise is the right to exercise one's faculties to the best of his abilities so long as he does not interfere with the rights of others in what he is doing. Did British Columbia interfere with the rights of the Dominion of Canada? Is the development of the Columbia river in British Columbia affecting the rights of the province of Alberta or of the province of Saskatchewan? Is it affecting any other part of Canada? Can we transport the water from the Columbia river in British Columbia to any other province? Is it possible to take the power and send it across the mountains? Are those mountains of such a nature that we could send the power through to Calgary? We know that the answer is "no". It is not feasible.
Canada is not doing that. She did not have the right to do it before. Now we suddenly find that it becomes necessary to take that right from British Columbia, to challenge her and her rights. Where are these champions of liberty, truth and justice? I am looking for them, for those people who always say that they are giving the true story.
Look at your newspapers right across this country and see how much of a national problem this thing is. I defy you to find more than half a dozen papers, even the local newspapers of Vancouver, devoting more than a relatively small space to it. That is how national it is. I wonder if it is because this little happy group of men here are trying to bring out the truth to the people. I do not think so. Maybe it is in the national interest that we should squelch all this talk against Bill No. 3 and its enactment into law. Possibly we should have a law that the Social Credit group should be squelched on this particular occasion.

speechtext:
I am ready to give the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) an opportunity to tell us all about the press act. He might be able to introduce a bill into the house, and as he is a Liberal I am satisfied it will get a more careful scrutiny than one we might present to the house. We would then have the privilege of discussing the Alberta press act or any other press act that has ever been brought into existence in days gone by.
I want to know where are those champions of liberty, truth and justice, the defenders of these things. Those people who in weeks past were ready to get up to speak about a human bill of rights would be well advised to ask themselves how you can get a human bill of rights if you are going to vest everything in the power of the national government. If you want a human bill of rights you must give the provinces their bill of rights, you must give the local districts their bill of rights.
I do not want to labour that point, but there is an important factor involved in these things. Every time we get centralization of authority within the centre of this government or any other government we give away a part of our own particular human rights, especially when it affects only one particular province as does this bill.
There is one further step. I mentioned earlier the responsibility of members of parliament. I should like to ask the indulgence of the house to quote certain excerpts from bills and debates which have been brought up in this house in past years. One debate I should like to refer to is that of the parliament of Canada on confederation in 1865 and also the debates during the session of 1877. These are books that are revered by Canadian citizens everywhere. In years gone by I have frequently wondered what particular value there was in the teaching of history, but I think I found its particular purpose at this time.
There were certain fundamentals and principles that make up the basis for confederation and we should keep these in mind. When we think of this Dominion of Canada we must remember that it is not made up of just one or two particular provinces; it is the dominion as a whole. First, I should like to refer to page 377 of the debates of 1865 when the Hon. Mr. Langevin, who was
1482	HOUSE OF
International Rivers
solicitor general and from Quebec, spoke. At that time the province of New Brunswick had export licences on timber and when they came into confederation they wanted that right to be retained. Mr. Langevin said:
As to New Brunswick, the duty on the article in question is their principal revenue, as coal is almost the sole revenue of Nova Scotia; and if they had been deprived of them, they would have peremptorily refused to join the confederation.
I do not hear anybody applauding now, out at that time the report indicates "hear, tear". If the government which was formed at that time had taken from the province of New Brunswick the right to export its timber or had denied that right to Nova Scotia those two prdvinces would not have joined confederation at that time. Mr. Langevin then went on to say:
Their demand was perfectly just, and could not be refused.
Then on March 28, 1871, as reported in column 661 of the debates of that day, Sir George Cartier, a commoner of that day, when speaking on the bill to admit the province of British Columbia into confederation, had this to say:
He invited the freest and fullest discussion on each and every clause but he would remind them that the bill was in the nature of a treaty . . .- that the amendment of one paragraph or one item of those terms would defeat the whole project.
When British Columbia came into confederation she came in under a form of treaty. Members in the house at that time considered that a form of treaty. I am satisfied that they did it for only one purpose, to protect the rights of that particular province.

This is an amendment to that. It is taking from that power and right what was theirs at that day. British Columbia was happy to come into confederation because her rights were not being tampered with at that time. She sacrificed a lot to become a member. We hear people say peanuts, that it is a sell-out, that it is a steal when referring to this particular deal. Unfortunately I am not a constitutional lawyer nor a lawyer of any kind. If I were I might have more of these things at my fingertips and be able to refer to them as so many hon. gentlemen of the two senior parties in this house are able to do. On April 3, 1871, as reported in column 777 of the debates of that day, Mr. Campbell, a member, said that British Columbia gave to the railway a continuous grant of 20 miles on each side of the railway. That was the grant that was given. Was that a steal? How much was the property worth even at that time? Well over $50 million. What did Ontario do in comparison? She

The customs duty collected under the tariff of the colony amounted to $350,000,-
Note this closely.

Why were they willing to give this? So these rights would not be taken from them.
I wonder, as has been said before, if the same treatment has been accorded to British Columbia as is and has been accorded, let us say, to the other provinces in respect of the development of the St. Lawrence waterway project. I wish at this time to come relevantly to the matter of water itself. I have in my hand a copy of a minute of a report of the committee of the privy council approved by His Excellency the Governor General on June 19, 1947. The purpose behind this order in council was to outline the policy in respect of water rights between the provinces and the federal authority. Let us see what they had to say in 1947 in the privy council order:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated June 17th, 1947, from the Minister of Agriculture, representing that in connection with the construction of such large water development projects by the prairie farm rehabilitation organization as are approved by the governor in council and for which funds are provided by parliament it is desirable-
Note this.
-that the respective responsibilities of the dominion and of the province in which a project is constructed should be clearly defined and the procedure to be followed in regard thereto be established:
Lest someone say that this has to do with agriculture and possibly irrigation, may I say that so has the Arrow lakes project.
The committee, therefore, on the recommendation of the Minister of Agriculture, advise that Your Excellency may be pleased to approve the following principles to govern the policy of the dominion in respect to such projects:
1.	Before Canada undertakes the construction and operation of a project it will be necessary for the province in which the project is located to enter into an agreement:
(1)	to transfer any water rights required for the construction and operation of such project;

- (3) under which the water will be utilized by the province or some other authority or organization on the terms set out in such agreement. Thereafter, Canada will at the cost of Canada proceed with the construction of its share of the project at the earliest possible date.

Canada will make a legal survey of any lands necessary for the construction, operation and maintenance of the portion of any project to be constructed by Canada pursuant to this policy and will file a plan or plans of such survey in the appropriate land titles office and in the water resources office of the province.
4.	In the construction of an irrigation project hereunder Canada will undertake and assume responsibility for the construction of the main reservoirs and any connecting canals, and will be responsible for the maintenance and operation of such works; Canada will deliver to the province such water as it is agreed the province will utilize at such place and for such fee as may be agreed upon between Canada and the province. If the province does not desire to utilize all of such water Canada may enter into arrangements with others for the delivery and use of any water not taken by the province.

Total population in 1861-
He was referring to Canada.
-was 3,300,000 souls, and of these the total number of Catholics amounted to 1,494,000. Thus they will be numerous enough to protect their religious and other interests: and those interests will be in

a position of safety in the local legislatures. We do not seek to be allowed privileges which others have not-
But notice this.
-we only wish that our rights may be respected as we respect those of others.
That was the purpose of the members of the House of Commons at that time, namely to protect the rights of local interests. This, sir, is a local provincial problem, and we should be protecting the rights of the province. These words are just as applicable to British Columbia today as they were at the time when confederation was being brought about. Further, the hon. solicitor general had this to say, as found at page 384:
History is before us to prove that there will always be an opposition-
I should like the members of the official opposition to recognize that.
-and that if an attempt is made to oppress any one section of the confederation, its representatives would unite in a body with the minority, and having thereby constituted a majority, would prevent any injustice on the part of the federal government.
If the official opposition dies, we will do the job for them. Where is this unity when there is oppression of one province? Our province is claiming that it is being oppressed in this particular respect, and yet we find that because half a dozen other members of our group who come from the province of Alberta rise to help to defend us they are castigated for their action. I say "hear, hear" to them. Is it just that British Columbia's one great natural resource should be sacrificed to the rest of the dominion through the introduction of this bill? The federal authority apparently has set itself up as judge and without discussion has decided against the provincial authority. We find that to be very true. Certain cabinet ministers made specific remarks as to the deal that the province of British Columbia was consummating.
Where are these mouths that were going to speak so much in favour of the protection of provincial rights? I say they are indeed dumb mouths whose lips are sealed in mute evidence that this whole thing was set up under a false premise.
The hon. solicitor general Langevin, as found at page 368 of the proceedings of February 21, 1865, also had this to say:
Under confederation-
Remember, this is the confederation that British Columbia entered in 1871.
-there will no longer be domination of one race over another, and if one section should be desirous of committing an act of injustice against another section, all the others would unite to prevent it.
Where are these people who will stand up and speak to prevent the injustice that the

government of British Columbia claims is being perpetrated against them? I should like to re-emphasize before I take my seat that this is not and should not be a fight with respect to the merits of the Kaiser dam, but rather we should try to present the problem of provincial autonomy and provincial rights as they exist in the minds of the people of the province of British Columbia, in our own minds and, in fact, in the mind of everyone in this dominion.
I have one final statement which I believe deserves close scrutiny. It is found in sessional paper No. 18 tabled in 1871, and is a letter to Governor Musgrave of British Columbia, datelined Ottawa, February 1, 1871. It reads:
The terms of union are in nature of a treaty. They have been extensively published in Canada, and accepted by British Columbia. The Canadian government, therefore, think they have no right to alter those terms. After acceptance by Canada, parliament may, in its discretion, modify the tariff on the request of British Columbia. I have no doubt that parliament will consider any proposition made by you, with a desire to meet your views as much as it properly can.
The letter is signed by Lord Lisgar.

Canada, of course, is a federation. It is a federation in which power is shared, and

within the constitution certain stated authority rests with the provinces, and the central parliament is free to legislate in other fields. Section 92 of the British North America Act designates provincial rights. In clause 10 we find this:
Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:
(c) such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
I suggest there is a very delicate situation existing here. It seems to me as though the needle is very delicately poised. Before this parliament invokes this particular provision and exercises this overriding authority, it should very carefully consider its position. It has been suggested that this is a borderline case or an item in the twilight zone. Evidently this parliament must legislate before it can rob the province of certain rights and exercise authority over these particular types of works. The procedure, I suggest, will have a devastating effect upon dominion-provincial relations. At the moment, the federal government does not have the constitutional authority, otherwise they would not be introducing this particular measure.
Not only, Mr. Speaker, does the federal government not have the constitutional authority, but I suggest it does not have the ethical or moral right at this juncture to invade the fields of authority the provinces have been exercising-I may say, without challenge by this federal government-throughout the years. the provincial governments, British Columbia or any other government, are best qualified to decide what procedures are best, what matters are best, in the interests of the people. They are working with the problems day by day, and they are seized with the responsibility. The responsibility has been committed to them by the people of the respective provinces and they are held accountable by those same people for the faithful discharge of those obligations. I would suggest, therefore, that this bill is predicated on the assumption that the provincial government is neither capable nor desirous of developing the resources in the best interests of the people of Canada.

It would be surprising, yes. However, as I have said, we are not challenging the right of the dominion government to legislate on matters clearly in their jurisdiction. There is a division of jurisdiction; that is desirable and necessary. But we are objecting to the passage of a measure meant, no doubt as an emergency clause, to take from the provinces authority which is rightfully theirs.
During this debate in the last few days this matter of dominion-provincial relations has come up quite often. It came up in connection with educational grants, in the debate on the bill of rights. This government agreed with the principle that there must be a recognition and acknowledgment of provincial rights and provincial autonomy. Now, why bring in this measure to expropriate rights that have been exercised by provincial governments in the past?
I think there is an inherent danger here, because we have not been told to what extent this will be carried out.
I would like to ask the question: What proposed development is next going to fall under the disapproving frown of this government? What provincial rights are going to be whittled away next? There has been some talk about the diversion of flood waters from the Columbia into the Fraser river. I shall not debate the merits or demerits of that suggestion; but, in the event of a provincial government objecting to that, what is the federal government going to do? Will they pass another measure and say, "Whether you like it or not, we are going to do it." I think it involves the very same principle and the same situation.
I would like now to refer to a statement made by General A. G. L. McNaughton when he appeared before the committee on external affairs last year. This is a rather general statement. I do not think there is any controversy about it, but I would like to place it

on the record. General McNaughton said this, as recorded at page 168 of the proceedings of the standing committee on external affairs:
In dealing with British Columbia we feel we are dealing with views that are the consensus of views of all the people in that province, and I think when you have views with that sanction behind them, that they are views to which we must all pay the greatest attention: they have to be given every weight in the considerations that come forward in the international field.
Now, I have read that because I feel it is the basis of all successful dominion-provincial relations. They must be founded upon mutual respect for the rights of the respective jurisdictions, and a refusal to be led into the position of encroaching upon those respective jurisdictions, except by mutual consent and understanding. Bill No. 3 is far-reaching in its implications. As I have said, it will be looked upon as absolutely indefensible interference with provincial prerogatives.
Perhaps I now pass into the realm of the imaginary, if you wish to call it that-but let us suppose this bill is passed and any province refuses to recognize and acknowledge its validity. I think this matter was brought to our attention some few days ago by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) when he intervened in the debate and asked just how the penalties were going to be imposed, if the bill was passed. He asked how it was going to be enforced if a provincial government refused to recognize its validity. Well, we have the penalties outlined in the bill-and I understand at this stage I must not read them. But we do know there is a provision for fine and imprisonment.
Would it be possible to enforce those penalties in the event of a provincial government refusing to recognize the authority of the federal government in this respect? Would it be advisable to try it? Would it be wise to put this measure on the statute books, with that question in mind? Just how far could we go in the imposition of those particular penalties? The question has been asked as to who is going to arrest whom? It would be interesting to see just what would happen, if somehow or other a way was worked out whereby this could be enforced, to see the custodians of the law going into the province of British Columbia or any other province, enforcing the regulations, taking premiers and cabinet ministers and putting them in the pokey. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) said the other day, no doubt it would precipitate something almost like a civil war right in Canada's front yard.
Perhaps the Minister of Justice (Mr. Gar-son) will accede to the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver East and shed a little

light on the problem from that constitutional angle. I believe if this government goes ahead, against the considered judgment of the provincial government and the will of the people of British Columbia, then the Liberal party will be about as dead as a mackerel. In fact it will be about as dead as the Conservative party in that province at the present time. And the Minister of Fisheries will no doubt be right there.

This, and a good many other things that have gone on, or have failed to be done, indicate quite clearly to me the singular aversion on the part of this government, or of any minister of this government, to go to the authorities in British Columbia to try to get the truth on any one of these matters. That is perfectly correct. There has been no effort on their part to go to the authorities in British Columbia for information, or for the purpose of trying to work out the basis of co-operation to get this whole matter cleared away, not the slightest. If there has been, no one on the other side of the house has attempted to place the information before this house so that we would know it. And yet the minister rises in his place today and reads this long telegram in which he emphasizes the information which he got to the effect that no contract was signed between the Bonneville authority and Kaiser, and therefore he deduces, by inference, at any rate, that there is no possibility of the Kaiser deal being enforceable.
Well, now, Mr. Speaker, nobody here or anywhere else that I have known, except on the opposite side of the house, has said that there was a contract. I thought I made it abundantly clear when I spoke on February 11-and finally it was noted, at any rate, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because he mentioned it in his closing speech on the night of February 11-that I went to the province of British Columbia and obtained information which I put on the record.


I am just going to refresh the memory of the minister, for whom I have high regard. For us, at any rate, it is a matter of principle, and I think he is on the wrong end of the principle this time. I said, as reported at page 1092 of Hansard, in relation to this very question:
Here are some of the things the minister could have found out if he had made the slightest effort to put himself on speaking terms with the British Columbia administration, which he did not. As the minister knows, the present Kaiser agreement is mainly exploratory. It does not pretend to be final in all respects. Before it is finalized, there will be a contract between Kaiser and Bonneville which will be assigned to the government of the province of British Columbia. Guarantees with respect to the delivery of power, and the posting of the performance bond to guarantee delivery, are all part and parcel of a conditional water licence which can contain any terms and conditions which the province may wish to impose.
The performance bond will be issued by a reliable bonding company and will guarantee either the delivery of the stipulated amount of power in British Columbia or, in case of bankruptcy or failure of the company, a cash payment equal to the value of the electricity over the entire 50 years.
Now, everybody who knows anything about this situation at all must realize that nobody has claimed that there is a firm contract signed. Nobody claimed there was a contract between Bonneville and Kaiser.

It is a lot different from what other people have done with little excuse. It must be perfectly clear to anyone who has done any thinking at all about the manner in which the government has dealt with the province of British Columbia and the whole waters problem in that province that it has been unjust and unfair and unwise, and in many respects politically despicable; that it has caused much disunity in our country at a time when unity is so essential to our preservation and development.
I think that I am safe in saying also that the way the government rushed Bill No. 3 before the house exposes the purpose that was behind it, that is to block a deal between Her Majesty in the right of the province of British Columbia and a private corporation. That has caused widespread fear about what this or some other reckless government in the future may be tempted to do if they do not like something that a province is trying to do toward developing its own resources.
This business of federal action directed against a province is what we have been fighting. Federal action in this parliament directed against a province and what it is doing is something which the Canadian people will not tolerate if they come to realize the facts about what is really going
International Rivers
on. It is because we were anxious to see that the people from one end of the country to the other had a chance to get the details of what was going on that we have conducted this debate. I will say that there has been no element whatsoever in it of a desire to hold up this bill simply for the satisfaction of holding it up; not for a moment. The people of Canada by and large are very fair and just in their judgment. I am ready to leave the matter of judgment to them. They are most jealous also of their local rights.
As the details of the present situation filtered through to them, I know from my own experience that the people felt angry about how this government was attempting to throw sand into the gears of provincial development machinery at this time and in this manner. Hon. members opposite deny that there was any attempt by the federal government to use this bill as a means of blocking a deal. I have heard that said, but the pertinent facts prove that such a denial is unfounded and support our contention that Bill No. 3 was rushed in-I stress the word "rushed"-as it was and when it was for, among other things, and this was very prominent among the other things, the purpose of blocking the Kaiser deal
wnat are the facts that indicate that clearly? The first is that this bill was mentioned in the speech from the throne and immediately afterward, far more quickly than on any other occasion that I have known of it was introduced into this house and a statement was made which indicated that there was a real rush and that the house should deal with it quickly.

That may be true; I do not know about that. The objection to what British Columbia has done on the basis of their alleged failure to consult General McNaughton is ill-founded. This was not a matter for the international joint commission, not at all; this was a matter for consultation and negotiation between the government of British Columbia and the government of Canada. General McNaughton made his position abundantly clear in his evidence before the external affairs committee last year. I just take time to quote briefly what he said at page 174 of the evidence. He was being questioned by the hon. member for Vancou-ver-Quadra (Mr. Green):
Q. Then you mentioned Mica creek and various other potential developments. By what authority would those have to be built? Would they be the responsibility of the dominion, the provincial government or private enterprise, or just how would they be built?
Then General McNaughton's answer was as follows:
A. No sir, the commission's responsibility under the reference is an over-all plan to develop the particulars and details right down to and including the designs of the particular works needed. We are doing that. As regards Mica creek, we have had the additional survey information, that we so badly needed, made available to us, within the past few months.
And so on. Then he goes on to say this:
So from the commission point of view, that project could be cleared for construction at any time within a year. The people to build it, the responsibility of building that dam, lies with the provincial government. They must say whether they are going

to build it themselves through the B.C. Power Commission or whether they are going to bring in a group of private interests to build it. All these things are very definite possibilities, but the decision will lie with the provincial government.
General McNaughton realized only too well that the international joint commission's responsibility was, first, negotiation with the United States division of the international joint commission with a view to some international agreement within the scope of their authorities; second, to develop plans to the last detail for the development of any one of these powers and to make them available to the authority that was to build them. So this was not a question of reference to General McNaughton. It was not the responsibility of the province of British Columbia to consult with General McNaughton about it. If there was any consultation to go on at all, it was between the British Columbia government and the appropriate division of the government of Canada.
I think that General McNaughton had no reason to feel piqued at what British Columbia had done. He may have felt concerned and one could understand that perhaps if he had plans in his mind. But it would seem to me that, with those plans in his mind, what he should have suggested to the minister or ministers of the crown here is this:	Why do
you not get out there or have those people come down here, sit down and talk this thing over and arrive at some sort of agreement so that we can go ahead without having a lot of trouble? That could have been done. I say this to you, Mr. Speaker: Personal pique or anger is not a good reason for bringing in any bill with the tremendous implications contained in this bill, which invokes a clause in the constitution that should be used most sparingly and then only after the fullest consultation with the provinces that are now or might later be affected by that legislation. If the federal government or any official of it was angry about what British Columbia was trying to do, it was clearly a matter between them and Her Majesty in the right of the province of British Columbia. This government should have communicated any disapproval they may have had to the British Columbia government. Did they do that?

indicate any disapproval of plans to build a dam to store water in the Arrow lakes. If they did, they have certainly kept it a deep dark secret.
I should like just to go back for one minute to this question of principle. A good deal has been said about the principle of the bill and what it is. I do not intend to go over all of it because there is another thing that has not been touched yet; no reference has been made to it. This to me is a matter of principle. One part of the bill-under the rules I am not permitted to say which part that is-declares that all international river improvements heretofore or hereafter constructed, and not excepted from the operation of this act are hereby declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada. That is, of course, the exercise of the power of expropriation by one government from another. The only way that very great power-and I say it is a very great power- can be granted is by majority vote of the people's representatives in this parliament. If we pass Bill No. 3, then we give this parliament practical ownership-and I want this noted particularly-of all of the defined works on all the international rivers of Canada. But I wonder whether it has occurred to hon. members-whether it has not struck them as rather peculiar, as a matter of fact-that if this government has induced this parliament to grant it drastic powers of expropriation by invoking section 92 (10) of the British North America Act, they would ask parliament at the same time to give the governor in council the right to set aside the declaration made in clause 9 by the powers asked for in clause 3.
To me that is a mighty serious point of principle and is a mighty serious business. It is a principle which should never be countenanced by the parliament of a free country. That is one more right good reason why we are opposed to the principle of this bill.
My friend the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra this afternoon said that this is a bill which is just perfect to be studied by a committee. Well, maybe it is, but why in the world rush to get it to the committee before we understand what the principle is? We are discussing the principle here today, and if the bill gets to the committee then that is an indication that the house has approved the principle. That is what will be thrown up to us. It will be said: Well, you agreed in principle by a majority vote. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that becomes more serious when the principle has not been fully explored as yet.

subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Northwest Territories Act to increase the sessional indemnity of elected members of the Northwest Territories council.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is proposed to increase the indemnities of the elected members of the Northwest Territories council. The level of those indemnities was set in 1951 when the Northwest Territories Act was amended to provide for the first time for the election of members to the council from that part of Canada which now comprises the Northwest Territories. It has become apparent that the important responsibilities and work of the elected members of council warrant the payment of a higher scale of indemnities, and it is proposed to make the required amendment to provide for this.
With the present scale the members now receive $50 a day for each day they are in attendance and the maximum in a year is

$1,000. It is proposed to increase the daily indemnity to $100, with the maximum increase to $2,000 a year.
An additional minor amendment is proposed to clarify the powers of the commissioner in council of the Northwest Territories to appropriate moneys from the Northwest Territories revenue account which have been credited to the account from time to time by vote of parliament. It is to clarify the power of the commissioner of the Northwest Territories to appropriate the moneys which have come not only from territorial revenues, but those which he has received under the tax rental agreement that exists between the federal government and the Northwest Territories government.

subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
I am glad that the government has introduced this resolution and the legislation which will be consequent upon it. The number of people in the Northwest Territories is increasing and will continue to increase, and the responsibilities of the elected members will increase constantly also. Their constituencies are extremely large, and it seems only reasonable that they should have an increase in their indemnity, both in the amount of the daily indemnity for the sessions they attend and the maximum which they can secure.
If I understood the minister correctly, this same piece of legislation is going to provide for some change in the power of the commissioner, which is not mentioned in the resolution. Perhaps I misunderstood the minister in that regard, because I see him shaking his head. His remarks in regard to the power of the commissioner to allocate funds apply to a different piece of legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext: I wish to assure my hon. friend that it is, as I said, only a clarification, because the commissioner in council of the Northwest Territories has already in the past appropriated funds which were received under the tax rental agreement. But because of the wording of the present act, we thought it would be better to clarify his position in that connection. I cannot refer to the bill at this time or its clauses, but I can assure the committee that this is only a clarification. There is no change in the powers of the commissioner in council.

subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
This particular resolution has to do with an amendment to the Northwest Territories Act in respect to an increase in the salaries of the elected members of the council. The resolution immediately preceding this one on the order paper is an almost identical resolution and has to do with an amendment to the Yukon Act. It asks precisely the same thing in so far as the salaries 50433-951
Northwest Territories Act are concerned. I am sure that hon. members are always anxious to expedite the work of the house. Possibly for that reason some latitude might be given in discussing the resolution before us if a reference is made to the Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext: The next item of business announced by the leader of the house last night is the resolution which precedes a bill to amend the Yukon Act.

subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext: The only reason I mentioned it was that I thought we could avoid repetition.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext: It is the next order of business.

subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
If one is satisfied that the present type of administration seems to be the best in so far as the Northwest Territories are concerned, and that the present administration does carry out satisfactorily law, order and good government of the territories, one could not do anything but agree with the minister's proposal that an increase in the salaries of the elected members of council is in order. However, I do not hold that view entirely. I believe a better system of administration could be devised, and I should like to say something about that for a moment, because I believe it is relevant to the discussion.
In the light of the tremendous development that has taken place, and is taking place in the territories, I hope the government will give consideration to setting up in the north a type of government similar to what we have in the provinces. They should have provincial status.
It must be obvious that the present administration in that area has outlived its usefulness and to all intents and purposes has become obsolete. I believe it is time that the northland was given provincial status in order to facilitate the tremendous development that is going on there at the present time.
As I said a moment ago, the present administration is unable to cope with the rapid growth of that area. Certainly the present salaries paid to the elected members of the Northwest Territories council is not much of an incentive to them to accept and carry out their great responsibilities. It is obvious that they are acting only in a very minor advisory capacity to the commissioner, who in the case of the Northwest Territories is appointed by order in council and is the deputy minister of northern affairs and national resources.
This observation seems to be borne out by the facts. Last year the Northwest Territories council met three times. They met
1496	HOUSE OF
Northwest Territories Act once in Yellowknife for a five-day session when they passed 55 bills, 17 of which were substantial amendments to existing ordinances. The second session which was held at Ottawa lasted five days, at which 17 major pieces of legislation were dealt with. The third meeting was also held in Ottawa when the council sat for only one day and passed only one bill. It would seem obvious that these people became affected by the Ottawa atmosphere.
There may have been another reason in the fact that they are allowed only $1,000 a year.
I suppose after the first session, at which they felt they had given their best efforts when they passed 55 bills, the other sessions did not warrant as much effort. As I say, at the second session they passed 17 pieces of legislation, and at the last session which lasted for only one day they passed only one bill. Then again it may be that they used their powers of observation while in Ottawa. Possibly the house was sitting and they were able to see how bills were dealt with here.
The living allowance granted to members iof council is $15 a day with a maximum of :$200 in a year. I should like the minister to give some clarification of that and possibly comment upon why it is that the living allowance for the elected members of the Northwest Territories council is $15 per day while that for members of the Yukon council is only $10 per day. I wonder why there is that discrepancy.
No mention is made of the salary of the commissioner and possibly there could be some clarification there.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext: He is my deputy minister. He has his salary as deputy minister and is not paid as commissioner.

subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
Another thing we should have clarified is why it is that under certain circumstances members of the council will be able to claim their indemnity even if they are not able to attend the sessions. There must be some reason for this and I should like to hear the minister's comment.
There is another aspect on which I should like some comment by the minister because I find it hard to understand. Why is it that when a fine is imposed under the act, following a conviction for the illicit manufacture of alcohol in the territories, whoever acts as informer is awarded the total amount of the fine. I wonder what is the thinking behind that.
In conclusion I should like to say that I hope the government gives immediate and serious consideration to giving provincial


status to this northern part of Canada, making it the eleventh province of Canada. At the present time there are 15 elected members of the two territories, including the two commissioners. While I do not suggest that that number should be reduced under provincial status, I think that that form of government would be better and would be able to cope with the development that is taking place there much better than can be done under the existing system.
Speaking to the Canadian Club in Toronto on November 22, 1954, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) traced the history of these northern areas in detail, pointing out the tremendous developments that have taken place and are now taking place, and also spoke of their future possibilities. He pointed to the early development of the western provinces as having a parallel in the north of today.
Surely the formation of provincial governments early in the history of western Canada gave a great impetus to its spectacular development. There is every reason to believe that a similar impetus would result from giving provincial status to our northland. By so doing we would once again be exhibiting that same kind of spirit, the same kind of vision and the same courage.

subtopic: INCREASE IN INDEMNITY OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak on this resolution as I was happy to accept it as it was. I was glad to note that there is to be an increase in the indemnity of council members. I thought that when the bill was before us and we knew its contents I would speak, but as the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) has attempted to tell us what he knows about the Northwest Territories council I feel I should say a word.
The hon. member mentioned that last year there were three meetings of the Northwest Territories council. In 1954 there was one meeting of the council because that was an election year. That meeting was held in Yellowknife.
As a former member of the council I am glad that the indemnities are being increased. These elected representatives have to cover fair-sized constituencies; mine was in the neighbourhood of 200,000 square miles. I remember receiving a cheque for the year from the Northwest Territories council for $200. I still do not know how they expected us to cover our constituencies and attend meetings of the council on $200.
I would like to suggest to the minister that when he brings the bill in he have it provide a minimum of at least $1,000 a year.

That would enable the members of the council to visit their constituencies and I think it would be a fair minimum.
As far as the maximum is concerned, I think $3,000 would be adequate. I am not so much interested in the maximum, but some provision should be made in regard to the minimum. I just wanted to straighten out the hon. member across the way on the meetings held in 1954.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Mr. Lesage thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 179, to amend the Northwest Territories Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Lesage (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Yukon Act to increase the indemnity and the living allowance to be paid to members of the Yukon council while in attendance at a session of the council and to provide that under certain conditions a member shall be deemed to be in attendance at a session.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the new Yukon Act provides for payment of indemnities for each day's attendance in council sessions and for an annual limitation on the total amount of indemnity that can be paid to each member on the same basis as that at present in effect in the Northwest Territories. The bill which has just been introduced to amend the Northwest Territories Act provides for an increase in the indemnity paid to the elected members of the Northwest Territories council. It is considered that the same new basis should apply to the members of the Yukon council who are all elected, as hon. members know.
It is also proposed to increase the daily living allowance to $25-and I should like to draw this to the attention of my friend the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson)-which will put the living allowance in the Yukon on the same basis as that in the Northwest Territories, and to provide for the payment of these allowances on days when council is in session but is adjourned for the day. We amended the Northwest Territories Act to that effect at the last session. This provision would bring the payment of living allowance to members of the Yukon council
Yukon Act
into line with that provided for members of the Northwest Territories council following the amendment that was passed in this house last year.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure you will agree that the increase in indemnities for members of the Yukon territorial council is long overdue. I am certainly pleased that the minister is bringing in this resolution, and I am happy to support it.
The present council consists of five members who understand the problems of our northland, having resided for many years in the Yukon where they brought up their families. These men have vision and possess high integrity and ability to deal with the various problems with which we have to contend in the north. We in the Yukon are extremely fortunate in having elected members of their calibre and understanding to represent us. I hope that the proposed bill, when introduced, will make provision for a substantial increase in the indemnities and bring them into line with those paid to members of the legislative assemblies of the various provinces.
One of the hon. members who spoke on the previous bill mentioned the fact that the Northwest Territories should have provincial status at this time. I think at the same time he was probably referring to the Yukon Territory. I have been thinking along those lines for quite some time. There is nothing that would please me better than to see both territories given provincial status. The time is coming-I believe within another ten years-in the Yukon when we will be in a position to accept provincial status; but right now, Mr. Chairman, we have not the population or the industry to support a provincial government. In other words, we are practically wards of the federal government and we must get along with them for a while, much as I should like to see the situation otherwise.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just as there was a good case for increasing the indemnity for the elected members of the Northwest Territories council, similarly there is a good case as far as the Yukon is concerned. I am sure that everyone in this party is convinced that that action should be taken and thus is in agreement with the proposed legislation.
There is, however, one thing on which I should like to have a little bit of clarification from the minister. As I understand it, the present payments in the Yukon are in the amount of $1,000 as far as each session of the council is concerned at which a member is in attendance, and an amount of $10 a day for expenses. That is the provision under

Yukon Act
the revised statutes of 1952. But there is in existence a further act which was passed in 1952-53 and which provides for $50 a day up to a maximum of $1,000 and $15 a day expenses. Apparently this legislation will only come into effect on the 1st of April this year. I wanted to ask the minister if the same situation is going to prevail so far as this new legislation is concerned; that is, is it going to be some two years before it comes into effect? Or, from the practical point of view, is the legislation which was passed in the 1952-53 session and which would normally come into effect on April 1 of this year, the legislation under which these people are going to be compensated or is this new legislation going to come into effect immediately?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext: The amendment that I am now proposing is to the act which will come into effect on April 1. There is no point in amending the act which will be in force from this date until April 1 only, since there will not be any session of the council, according to my information. But the new act, which is chapter 53 of the statutes of 1952-53, will come into force on April 1. When it comes into force on April 1, it will come into force as amended by the bill which will be introduced. following the adoption of this resolution.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext: I wonder whether the minister can tell why it has not been in effect before this time? Can he tell us why two years have elapsed since it was passed and it has not yet gone into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext: Because with regard to the Yukon Act as well as the Northwest Territories Act which are presently in force there are certain provisions which do not appear in the new acts but are covered under the new Criminal Code. We could not have the new Yukon Act and the new Northwest Territories Act come into force before the new Criminal Code comes into force, which is on April 1.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext: First of all, I should like to say that I was in error when I spoke about three sessions having to do with the Northwest Territories. Nevertheless that is a true statement in connection with the Yukon Act. I was glad to hear the comments made by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Simmons) with respect to provincial status. I think the fact that these men met for five days and passed 55 pieces of legislation is a fair indication that they are under the influence of the deputy minister of northern affairs and national resources.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext: In the Yukon?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext: I am sorry, the commissioner, who is appointed by order in council. I should like to ask the minister two questions. First of all, what is being done about travelling allowances? If these people are going to come to Ottawa it is going to take considerable money. I wonder whether allowance is being made for that. Second, have the minister and his department given any active study to the proposition of provincial status for these territories?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
Members of the Yukon council have their travelling expenses paid to Whitehorse where all the meetings of the council are held. Meetings of the Yukon council are never held in Ottawa. They are always held in the capital of the Yukon which is Whitehorse. The travelling expenses of the members from their residences to Whitehorse are paid for each session.
As to the second question, I said last year in the house and I have said in public many times that our ultimate objective is to grant provincial status to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, but for the reasons that have been given by the hon. member for the Yukon we do not believe that the time has yet come. The population is too small and the revenues of these two territories are not sufficient to cover the expenditures that would have to be made for provincial services by the new provinces if they had provincial status at this time. There is only a population of 10,000 in the Yukon and 16,000 in the Northwest Territories. The population of the Northwest Territories is scattered not only in Mackenzie district, where the four elected members are elected, but also in Keewatin and Franklin districts. As a matter of fact, in the district of Mackenzie from which the elected representatives come, the non-Indian and non-Eskimo population is less than 5,000.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING LIVING ALLOWANCE AND ATTENDANCE OF COUNCIL MEMBERS
speechtext:
I do not want to enter into a general debate on this matter except to add a word to those of the hon. member for Mackenzie River a short time ago on the previous resolution when he asked the minister to consider inserting a provision in the bills for both territories for a minimum payment to the elected representatives. In order to get the best men for the job and to be assured that they will give proper consideration to their positions, it seems to me that a minimum payment would help a great deal. I think it is a good idea and I think it should be made applicable in the case of both bills.
